'''Yang Shi''' is a molecular biologist known for work on epigenetic regulation, particularly histone and RNA methylation.<ref name="Epi Explorer">{{cite web |title=The epigenetic explorer |url=https://www.ludwigcancerresearch.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/11/The-epigenetic-explorer.pdf |website=Ludwig Cancer Research |access-date=7 May 2026}}</ref> He is a Member of the [[Ludwig Institute for Cancer Research]] and a professor at the [[University of Oxford]].<ref name="Shi Ludwig">{{cite web |title=Yang Shi |url=https://www.ludwigcancerresearch.org/scientist/yang-shi/ |website=www.ludwigcancerresearch.org |access-date=4 May 2026}}</ref> Shi is best known for his discovery of lysine-specific [[demethylase]] 1 (LSD1/KDM1A) in 2004, which demonstrated that histone methylation is reversible.<ref name="Cell 2004">{{cite journal |last1=Shi |first1=Yujiang |title=Histone demethylation mediated by the nuclear amine oxidase homolog LSD1 |journal=Cell |date=2004 |volume=119 |issue=7 |pages=941–953 |pmid=15620353 |url=https://www.cell.com/cell/fulltext/S0092-8674(04)01199-7?|access-date=4 May 2026}}</ref> His work has identified multiple histone demethylases and clarified their roles in gene regulation, cancer, and human disease, and has contributed to the ongoing development of epigenetic cancer therapies.<ref name="Cell 2025">{{cite journal |last1=Gray |first1=Zach |title=20 years of histone lysine demethylases: From discovery to the clinic and beyond |journal=Cell |date=2025 |volume=188 |issue=7 |pages=1747–1783 |pmid=40185081 |url=https://www.cell.com/cell/fulltext/S0092-8674(25)00211-9 |access-date=4 May 2026}}</ref> He is an elected member of the [[National Academy of Sciences]], the [[National Academy of Medicine]], and the [[Royal Society]], and a recipient of the [[Leopold Griffuel Prize]].

== Career ==
Yang Shi received his PhD from [[New York University]] in 1987, where his doctoral advisor was Eva Derman.<ref name="Epi Explorer" /> He then completed postdoctoral training in the laboratory of [[Thomas Shenk]] at [[Princeton University]].<ref name="Shi Ludwig" />

Shi began his independent research career at [[Harvard Medical School]] in 1991 as a tenure-track assistant professor and was promoted to full professor in the Department of Pathology in 2004. In 2009, he joined the Newborn Medicine Division at [[Boston Children's Hospital]], where he held the Merton Bernfield Professorship.<ref name="NAS" /> In 2018, he was appointed the inaugural C. H. Waddington Professor of Pediatrics at Harvard Medical School.<ref name="Waddington">{{cite web |title=Dr. Yang Shi honored with C.H. Waddington Professor of Pediatrics endowed chair |url=https://cellbio.hms.harvard.edu/news/dr-yang-shi-honored-ch-waddington-professor-pediatrics-endowed-chair |website=cellbio.hms.harvard.edu |access-date=5 May 2026}}</ref> In 2020, he joined the [[Ludwig Institute for Cancer Research]] at the [[University of Oxford]].<ref name="Shi Ludwig" />

==Contributions and Impact==

Shi’s work has advanced understanding of epigenetic regulation through the discovery of histone and RNA-modifying enzymes and proteins that recognize histone methylation states.<ref name="Epi Explorer" /> He is best known for identifying the first histone [[demethylase]], LSD1 (KDM1A), in 2004, demonstrating that [[histone methylation]] is reversible.<ref name="Cell 2004" /> His group subsequently identified a second family of histone demethylases<ref name="Cell 2006">{{cite journal |last1=Whetstine |first1=Johnathan |title=Reversal of Histone Lysine Trimethylation by the JMJD2 Family of Histone Demethylases |journal=Cell |date=2006 |volume=125 |issue=3 |pages=467–481 |pmid=16603238 |url=https://www.cell.com/fulltext/S0092-8674(06)00422-3 |access-date=7 May 2026}}</ref> and contributed to the characterization of multiple demethylases and their roles in gene regulation, cancer, and human disease. His studies have also shown that LSD1 regulates tumor immunogenicity and that its inhibition can enhance responses to immune checkpoint therapies in various models and induce therapeutic differentiation, informing the ongoing development of epigenetic cancer treatments.<ref name="Cell 2025" />  More recently, his work on [[RNA methylation]] has revealed roles for m6A in transcriptional regulation and the DNA damage response, and identified new enzymes involved in RNA methylation.<ref name="Mol Cell 2023">{{cite journal |last1=Sendic |first1=Erdem |title=RNA m6A methylation across the transcriptome |journal=Molecular Cell |date=2023 |volume=83 |issue=3 |pages=428–441 |pmid=36736310 |url=https://www.cell.com/molecular-cell/fulltext/S1097-2765%2823%2900026-6 |access-date=5 May 2026}}</ref>
